title: What Are Edibles? A Beginner's Guide to THC and CBD Edibles
h1: Cannabis Edibles 101: How They Work, Dosing and Storage
metaDescription: What are edibles? How THC and CBD edibles are made, why they kick in slowly, how to read Michigan labels, safe storage and how they compare with smoking.
excerpt: Edibles are foods and drinks infused with cannabis. They kick in later and last longer than smoking, so the label, a small serving and patience matter most.
keyTakeaways: Edibles are cannabis-infused foods and drinks; THC edibles are intoxicating, while CBD-dominant ones contain little THC.
Effects usually start 30 to 90 minutes after eating and peak around 2 to 4 hours, much later than smoking.
Michigan caps adult-use edibles at 10 mg THC per serving and 200 mg per package; start with one serving or less and wait.
Homemade edibles cannot be dosed precisely, and edibles can look like ordinary snacks.
Keep edibles in their child-resistant package, locked away, and never drive after taking one.
body:
What are edibles? They're foods and drinks infused with cannabis, anything from gummies and chocolate bars to drinks and cooking oils. Because you swallow them, THC takes a slower route through your gut and liver. That's why edibles usually take 30 to 90 minutes to kick in and last longer than smoking. The delay is the most important thing to understand before your first one. Here's how edibles work, how to read a Michigan label and how to store them safely.

## What Are Edibles? Foods, Drinks and Pantry Items

Edibles are any cannabis product you eat or drink. Makers infuse cannabis into an ingredient, usually a fat or oil, and that ingredient goes into the food. In Michigan's licensed market you'll find several types:

| Type | What to know |
|---|---|
| Gummies and chews | Michigan bans human, animal and fruit shapes, so expect squares, circles and other simple shapes; fruit flavors are fine |
| Chocolates and baked goods | Bars are often scored into servings |
| Hard candies, mints and lozenges | Michigan packaging can't use the word "candy" |
| Drinks | Capped at 10 mg of THC per serving and 100 mg per container |
| Tinctures and capsules | Measured with a dropper or as a set dose |
| Pantry items | Infused butter, oil, honey or sugar for cooking, which makes servings harder to measure |

For shopping tips by format, see our [THC drinks and edibles buyer's guide](/blog/thc-drinks-edibles-buyers-guide/).

## THC vs. CBD Edibles

THC is the main intoxicating compound in cannabis. CBD is a different cannabinoid that isn't known for producing a high. Edibles generally fall into three profiles:

- **THC-dominant:** the typical adult-use edible, labeled with its THC content.
- **Balanced:** similar amounts of THC and CBD, often sold as 1:1.
- **CBD-dominant:** mostly CBD with little THC.

Whatever the ratio, Michigan labels list both THC and CBD. If you take medications, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have a health condition, talk with a clinician before trying any cannabis edible. Michigan labels carry a pregnancy and breastfeeding warning for good reason.

## How Edibles Are Made

THC and CBD dissolve in fats and oils, which is why so many edibles start with butter or oil. The basic steps:

1. **Activate.** Raw cannabis contains mostly THCA, which heat converts into THC. This step is called decarboxylation.
2. **Infuse.** The activated cannabis, or a refined extract, is warmed with butter or oil so the cannabinoids move into the fat. Some makers blend extract straight into a sugar or drink base.
3. **Measure and test.** Licensed products are made in measured batches, tested by a lab that's named on the label, and labeled with their THC and CBD content.

## Why People Choose Edibles

- **No smoke.** Nothing is burned or inhaled.
- **A longer experience.** Effects last longer than they do with smoking.
- **Measured servings.** Licensed edibles list their THC content, which makes amounts easier to track than puffs.
- **Convenience.** They're easy to carry and don't leave a smoky smell behind.

## The Tricky Parts: Delayed Onset, Homemade Dosing, Look-Alikes

### Delayed onset

The classic edible mistake is impatience. Effects usually start 30 to 90 minutes after eating and peak 2 to 4 hours in. Someone who feels nothing at the one-hour mark may take more, then feel both servings at once. Researchers at RTI International flag this pattern as a common route to unpleasant experiences.

Your liver also converts THC into a potent compound called 11-hydroxy-THC, which shows up in higher amounts after eating than after inhaling. That may help explain why edibles can feel stronger and last longer. Drinks can behave a little differently; our guide to [THC drink and edible timing](/blog/thc-drinks-vs-edibles-timing/) explains.

### Homemade dosing

With homemade edibles, potency is always an estimate. THC per serving depends on the starting material's potency, how completely it was decarboxylated, how much was lost during infusion and how evenly the butter or oil was mixed into the batch. Two brownies from the same pan can differ. If you cook at home, our [cannabutter guide](/blog/canna-butter/) walks through the process. Assume every homemade serving is stronger than you think, start with a small piece and label the container.

### Look-alike risk

Out of the package, many edibles look like ordinary snacks. Michigan's rules help: edibles must come in opaque, child-resistant packaging, can't be shaped like people, animals or fruit, and can't be labeled as candy. Labels also carry the state's universal THC symbol and a warning to keep the product out of reach of children. Those protections only work while the edible stays in its package.

## How to Take an Edible: Setting, Food, Patience

- **Pick your time and place.** Choose a day with nowhere to drive and nothing important to do, at home or another private place where you're allowed to consume.
- **Eat a normal meal.** Food, especially fat, changes how much THC you absorb and when it peaks, so an empty stomach can make the same serving feel different.
- **Start with one serving or less.** Then wait at least 2 hours before deciding on more.
- **Keep it simple.** Skip alcohol and other substances the first time.
- **Have a plan.** Keep water and snacks handy, and have a friend nearby if it's your first time.

## Dosing Basics and Reading Per-Serving Labels

Michigan caps adult-use edibles at 10 mg of THC per serving and 200 mg per package. Medical edibles for registered patients can go up to 50 mg per serving. So one package often holds many servings, and a serving can be a single gummy or one square of a bar.

On a Michigan label, look for:

- **THC and CBD content,** with a note that actual values may vary by 10%
- **Activation time,** a reminder that effects take a while to begin
- **The testing lab and test date**
- **Warnings,** including that it's illegal to drive under the influence, plus the Poison Control number, 1-800-222-1222

Start low with one serving or less, then wait. Our [THC dosage guide](/blog/thc-dosage-guide/) explains how tolerance changes the picture. If a label is confusing, a budtender at any of our [Michigan stores](/dispensary-locations/) can walk you through it.

## Storage, Shelf Life and Child-Safe Containers

- Keep edibles in their original child-resistant package with the label on, so anyone can see what they are and how strong they are.
- Lock them up, away from children, pets and the regular snack shelf.
- Store them cool, dry and dark, since chocolate and gummies can melt or warp in heat. Our [guide to storing cannabis](/blog/how-to-store-marijuana/) has more tips.
- Label anything homemade with "contains THC" and the date.
- If a child eats an edible, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the child has trouble breathing or won't wake up. For a pet, call your veterinarian.

As for shelf life, the food in an edible ages like any snack, so follow any dates on the package. The THC also breaks down slowly over time, faster in heat and light.

## Edibles vs. Smoking: Absorption and Duration

| | Smoking or vaping | Edibles |
|---|---|---|
| How THC gets in | Through the lungs into the bloodstream | Through the gut, then the liver |
| First effects | Within minutes | 30 to 90 minutes |
| Peak | About 20 to 30 minutes | About 2 to 4 hours |
| How long it lasts | Tapers off within 2 to 3 hours | Longer, often several hours |
| 11-hydroxy-THC | Lower levels | Higher levels |

Neither route is harmless. Inhaling is easier to adjust in the moment, while edibles skip smoke but demand patience. Whichever you choose, plan a ride and never drive after using cannabis.

faq.q: Is it legal to drive after an edible in Michigan?
faq.a: No. Every Michigan cannabis label warns that it is illegal to drive a motor vehicle while under the influence of marijuana. The state's adult-use law also does not protect impaired drivers or allow using cannabis while driving. Because edibles peak hours after you eat them and can last much of the day, plan to stay in or line up a ride. Our [Michigan cannabis law guide](/cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/) covers the driving rules in more detail.

faq.q: Where is it legal to eat an edible in Michigan?
faq.a: On private property where it is allowed, such as your own home. Michigan bans consuming cannabis in public places, and property owners can prohibit it. Renters get some protection: a lease can ban smoking, but it cannot stop a tenant from lawfully possessing cannabis and consuming it another way, such as eating an edible. Hotels and other businesses can set their own policies.

faq.q: Do edibles lose potency over time?
faq.a: Slowly, yes. THC breaks down with time, and heat and light speed that up. In a four-year study of stored cannabis and hash, samples kept at room temperature lost THC steadily, faster when exposed to light. Samples stored dark and refrigerated or frozen did not show those significant changes. Keep edibles sealed, cool and dark, and follow any dates on the package.

faq.q: Why does eating first change how an edible feels?
faq.a: Because food, especially fat, changes absorption. In a controlled study, people who took THC capsules after a high-fat meal absorbed more THC overall and reached their peak later than when they took them on an empty stomach. So the same serving can feel different from one day to the next. Eat a normal meal, take one serving or less and wait.

claims.claim: Swallowed THC goes through the gut and liver; edibles take 30 to 90 minutes to start and peak 2 to 4 hours in, lasting longer than smoking
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5260817/ (Barrus 2016, RTI International, full text via NCBI E-utilities, 2026-10-24): "From the gut, Δ9-THC is absorbed into the bloodstream and travels via the portal vein to the liver, where it undergoes first-pass metabolism" / "initial psychoactive effect of edibles (30 to 90 minutes) ... longer-lasting, with a peak at 2 to 4 hours after ingestion"

claims.claim: Inhaled: effects within minutes, peak about 20 to 30 minutes, tapering within 2 to 3 hours
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5260817/ (Barrus 2016, RTI International, full text via NCBI E-utilities, 2026-10-24): "takes initial effect within minutes, and shows peak effect in about 20 to 30 minutes, with psychoactive effects tapering off within 2 to 3 hours"

claims.claim: Liver makes 11-hydroxy-THC, more potent and higher after eating than inhaling; may explain stronger, longer effects
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5260817/ (Barrus 2016, RTI International, full text via NCBI E-utilities, 2026-10-24): "11-OH-THC is more potent than Δ9-THC ... and appears in blood in higher quantities when Δ9-THC is ingested than when it is inhaled ... it may be responsible for the stronger and longer-lasting drug effect of edibles"

claims.claim: RTI International researchers flag taking more before onset as a route to unpleasant experiences
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5260817/ (Barrus 2016, RTI International, full text via NCBI E-utilities, 2026-10-24): "may consume a greater than intended amount of drug before the drug has taken effect, often resulting in profoundly adverse effects"; authors' affiliation: RTI International, Research Triangle Park, NC

claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5260817/ (Barrus 2016, RTI International, full text via NCBI E-utilities, 2026-10-24): "Heating is required to convert THCA into Δ9-THC" / "dissolves into the oily liquid, along with other cannabinoids ... (such as CBD)" / "The Δ9-THC dose in homemade products depends upon the concentration of THCA in the plant"

claims.claim: High-fat food changes absorption: THC capsules after a high-fat meal gave more total THC exposure and a later peak
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6922062/ (Lunn 2019 abstract via E-utilities, PMID 31872060; authors employed by a cannabis company): "The presence of high-fat food significantly enhanced time to peak plasma concentration (T max) and area under the curve (AUC0-24) for both THC and 11-OH-THC"

claims.claim: Four-year storage study: room-temperature samples lost THC steadily, light speeding it; dark refrigerated or frozen samples did not show those significant changes
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30901710/ (Zamengo 2019 abstract via E-utilities): conditions (A) light and room temperature, (B) darkness and room temperature, (C) darkness and refrigeration, (D) darkness and freezing; "Significant changes in the THC (degradation) and CBN (formation) content were detected under storage conditions A and B" / "temperature changed only the speed, light changed both the speed and the stoichiometry"
